article.overview:
A lunar radio navigation beacon is a transmitter placed on the lunar surface, or carried on a lander, that broadcasts a radio signal from a known or accurately measured position. Spacecraft, landers, rovers and astronauts can use the signal to estimate their own position, velocity or time. A surface beacon complements satellites in lunar orbit: it provides a fixed reference point close to where users operate, such as a landing region near the lunar south pole.

The clearest flown example found in the sources reviewed is NASA's Lunar Node-1 (LN-1), an S-band navigation beacon designed and built at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center. LN-1 flew on Intuitive Machines' IM-1 mission, whose Nova-C lander, Odysseus, touched down near the crater Malapert A on 22 February 2024 [1][2]. Because the lander touched down tilted, LN-1 could not run the continuous surface beacon it was designed for. Its surface transmissions totalled about 30 minutes [2][3]. Most of the documented value so far therefore comes from its cruise-phase operations and its short surface test.
article.description:
A lunar radio navigation beacon is a radio transmitter whose position is known, or can be determined, and whose signal carries information that a user can use to work out range, velocity or time. The beacon itself does not compute the user's position. The user's receiver makes measurements on the beacon signal and combines them with its own clock and motion models.

Two broad measurement types are relevant:

- **Ranging.** The receiver or a ground station compares the time at which a signal left the beacon with the time at which it arrived. Distance is the travel time multiplied by the speed of light. In one-way ranging the clocks at the two ends must be synchronised well enough to make the time difference meaningful.
- **Doppler tracking.** Relative motion between transmitter and receiver shifts the received radio frequency. Measuring that shift gives information about line-of-sight velocity.

The LN-1 documentation describes both: one-way pseudo-noise (PN) ranging and one-way and two-way Doppler comparisons [1][3]. The ION GNSS+ 2024 paper on LN-1 uses the term "surface pseudolites" in its title. In satellite navigation, a pseudolite is a ground-based transmitter that imitates a satellite navigation signal. The paper's exact scope is known from its title and abstract only [3].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The purpose of a lunar navigation beacon is practical rather than purely scientific. It supports positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) for Moon missions. NASA's LN-1 project describes a navigation beacon that could provide position, velocity and time references for spacecraft and surface assets, and could reduce reliance on the Deep Space Network (DSN) for navigation tasks [1]. NASA states that the wider intent is a network in which spacecraft and surface users can verify their positions, including orbiters, landers, astronauts and rovers [2].

Applications identified in the sources reviewed include:

- **Backup or augmentation of onboard navigation.** During LN-1's translunar cruise, it relayed positioning data to DSN sites, providing a backup to the IM-1 lander's onboard navigation system [2].
- **Surface position references.** A beacon with a known or surveyed location can help a user near the landing region determine where it is, independent of orbital satellites.
- **Demonstration of autonomous positioning software.** The Multi-spacecraft Autonomous Positioning System (MAPS) algorithms used by LN-1 were previously tested on the International Space Station in 2018 [2].
- **Support for the Artemis architecture.** NASA's Lunar Communications Relay and Navigation Systems (LCRNS) project is building a commercial network of lunar-orbit relay satellites to support lunar communications and, as part of the wider lunar infrastructure, navigation [4]. A surface beacon is one possible complement to that architecture. The LCRNS page itself does not describe surface beacons [4].
article.operating_principle:
Based on NASA's technical description, LN-1 is built from CubeSat-class components. Its elements include an SWIFT SL-X S-band transmitter, an FPGA-based controller board, power-conditioning electronics, a radiator hat and an antenna mount adapter [1]. The ION GNSS+ 2024 abstract states that the payload's one-way transmissions were disciplined by an onboard Space Chip Scale Atomic Clock, and that they were received by DSN receivers [3].

In operation, the beacon transmits navigation signals independently of the host lander, while commands and data pass between the beacon and the lander over a hardwired link [1]. LN-1 was designed to transmit continuously for a planned 7 to 10 days after landing [1][3]. The evaluation in the ION paper compared time-based transfer ranging and one-way PN ranging with one-way Doppler, two-way Doppler and visual verification of the landing site from orbit [3].

The operating principle of a surface beacon depends on the transmitter's position being known to a useful accuracy. If the beacon's position is fixed in advance, users need to track the beacon's own orbit less frequently than they must track a moving satellite. This is a general feature of surface-based references rather than a result specific to LN-1, and no quantitative trade study was reviewed for this article.

*A NASA concept of operations diagram, showing dual data paths between the payload and the lander, is published on the source page. Its direct image asset was not verified in this run, so it is referenced here rather than embedded. See [NASA Science, Deploying and Demonstrating Navigation Aids on the Lunar Surface](https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/science-enabling-technology/deploying-and-demonstrating-navigation-aids-on-the-lunar-surface) [1].*
article.scientific_importance:
A lunar navigation beacon is important because it tests how a position, velocity and time reference can be provided on the Moon, where GNSS satellites from Earth do not operate. The sources reviewed describe navigation on the Moon as essential for crewed missions, robotic missions, rovers and infrastructure development [4]. A surface beacon provides a local reference that is independent of orbital assets.

The scientific and engineering value of LN-1 is still being assessed. NASA stated in March 2024 that the team was still evaluating the data received through the DSN, and that LN-1 had produced telemetry, navigation measurements and other data [2]. The ION paper title and abstract indicate that the flight results are being used to explain the role of surface pseudolites in lunar navigation [3]. Quantitative positioning accuracy results were not found in the sources reviewed.

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal specification for a lunar radio navigation beacon. Beacon designs vary with frequency band, ranging method, clock, power source and mounting. The examples describe specific beacon or relay designs. They are not interchangeable, and figures should not be carried over from one to another.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: LN-1 dimensions are not reliably reported: the NASA project page gives 175x220x300 cm, which is inconsistent with its approximately 2.8 kg mass, so the value is not used. Lunar Pathfinder dimensions are not stated in the ESA article reviewed.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: LN-1 has an approximate mass of 2.8 kg, as stated on the NASA project page. Lunar Pathfinder's mass is not stated in the ESA article reviewed. Masses are not comparable between a surface beacon and an orbital relay.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: LN-1 power consumption is not publicly specified. NASA states that long-term surface operation would need adequate power generation or storage but gives no figures. The sources reviewed do not describe LN-1's power source in detail. Lunar Pathfinder power is not stated in the ESA article reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
A lunar surface beacon must survive a vacuum, large temperature swings between lunar day and night, radiation, and the mechanical loads of launch and landing. LN-1 was tested for vibration, EMI and thermal-vacuum conditions at NASA Marshall before flight [1]. NASA's project page states that LN-1 was not designed to survive the lunar night [1]. Continuous surface operation therefore depends on power generation or storage, which is not specified in the sources reviewed [1].

Radio operation also depends on geometry. The beacon's signal must be visible to the receiving station, whether that is a DSN antenna, a relay satellite or a user on the surface. Its antenna orientation therefore matters. In LN-1's case, the lander's tilt at touchdown reduced the surface transmission time to two short bursts [2][3].
article.limitations:
- **Limited surface operation.** LN-1 was designed for a 7 to 10 day continuous surface beacon, but it made two 15-minute transmissions because of the lander's attitude at touchdown [2][3].
- **Not designed for the lunar night.** LN-1 is not designed to survive the lunar night, so its surface life is limited by the lunar day [1].
- **Single-beacon limits.** A single beacon with a known position can help a user only with respect to that position. Full positioning requires a reference frame, a clock model and enough measurements for the user to solve for position.
- **Limited public accuracy data.** The sources reviewed did not publish a positioning accuracy figure for LN-1 [2][3].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A surface navigation beacon is a surface payload. Its transportation chain covers Earth integration, launch, lunar transfer, landing delivery, deployment, and power and data connections. LN-1 is the documented example: it was integrated on Intuitive Machines' NOVA-C lander for IM-1, which launched on 15 February 2024 and landed on 22 February 2024.
transportation_process: Earth integration: LN-1 was integrated onto the NOVA-C lander for IM-1. NASA's caption states that it was mounted near the top deck for antenna view.

Launch and lunar transfer: IM-1 launched on 15 February 2024. During translunar cruise LN-1 transmitted to the Deep Space Network near-daily and provided backup positioning data to the lander's onboard navigation.
Landing: Odysseus touched down on 22 February 2024 near Malapert A. The lander's tilt limited the surface transmissions.

Deployment and interfaces: LN-1 transmitted independently of the lander, while commands and data passed over a hardwired link. No separate deployment mechanism or antenna deployment sequence is described in the sources reviewed.
Power and thermal: LN-1's power source and thermal control design are not described in detail in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: LN-1 was carried on the lander and began transmitting after landing. No separate deployment mechanism is documented in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: LN-1 on IM-1 (2024) is the documented flown example in this article. The ESA and SSTL Lunar Pathfinder relay is a related lunar-orbit architecture whose launch status was not confirmed in this run.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: LN-1's integration with IM-1 is documented. Compatibility of a new beacon with any other lander, rover or spacecraft has not been assessed and should not be assumed without verified interface data.

article.historical_significance:
NASA reports LN-1 as a test of a self-directed navigation and positioning system designed to support a point-to-point network [2]. The IM-1 mission is described by NASA as the first American commercial uncrewed Moon landing [2].

NASA's account of the test notes that the DSN locked onto the beacon signal and received telemetry, navigation measurements and other data [2]. The team at Marshall, JPL and Morehead State University received that data and continued to evaluate it [2].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- **Lunar radio navigation beacon is a class name.** Designs differ in band, ranging method, clock, power source and mounting. Figures for LN-1 should not be applied to other beacons.
- **LN-1 flight results are preliminary.** The ION GNSS+ 2024 paper is a presentation whose abstract describes limited surface operations [3]. NASA's March 2024 article states that data analysis was ongoing [2].
- **LN-1 dimensions are unresolved.** The NASA page's dimension value is inconsistent with the stated mass [1]. No verified external dimensions were found.
- **LN-1 power and frequency are unresolved.** Power consumption and the specific carrier frequency were not stated in the sources read [1][3].
- **Surface accuracy is unpublished.** No positioning accuracy figure from LN-1 was found in the sources reviewed.
- **Date of the ION paper.** The paper record gives a conference date of 16 to 20 September 2024 but does not state a publication date on the page read [3].
- **Historical lunar beacon studies.** A 1989 NASA-hosted document on a spread-spectrum radio-beacon navigation concept was identified in search results. Its PDF was not readable in this run, so no claims from it are included in this article.
- **Lunar Pathfinder status.** Its launch date and navigation results were not confirmed from a current primary source in this run [5].
- **Lunar relay context.** The LCRNS project page was last updated 17 February 2026 and carries a notice that NASA was not updating the site during a federal funding lapse. Its status may not reflect the current situation [4].
- **Image rights.** Rights and reuse terms were not checked for any image. Credits are recorded where the source pages state them. The credit for the Anzalone photograph was not given on the page. Confirm usage terms before republication.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery. The concept of operations diagram on the NASA source page is referenced in the article text but not embedded, because its direct asset URL was not verified.

data_quality_notes: LN-1 dimensions: the NASA project page gives 175x220x300 cm, which is inconsistent with the stated 2.8 kg mass. The value is not used.
LN-1 power consumption and specific carrier frequency are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
Concept of operations diagram (dual data paths between payload and lander) is on the NASA source page but was not embedded. Its direct asset URL was not verified in this run.

Direct image URLs for the four embedded images returned image content on direct fetch in this run. Rights and reuse terms were not checked. The credit for the Anzalone photograph is not listed on the source page.
The Odysseus lander surface image shows the lander surroundings, not the LN-1 payload.
The LN-1 accuracy results are not published in the sources reviewed. NASA reported in March 2024 that data analysis was ongoing, and the ION paper describes limited surface operations.

Search-result summaries reported 15 minutes of one-way PN ranging from the lunar surface and about 4.5 hours of cruise-phase MAPS packets. These were not verified on a primary page and are not used in the article.
The ION GNSS+ 2024 paper publication date is not stated on the record read. The conference dates are used instead. The canonical URL was taken from search results and the NTRS record.

A 1989 NASA-hosted document on a spread-spectrum radio-beacon navigation concept (NTRS 19890009072) was identified in search results. Its PDF was not readable in this run, so no claims are drawn from it.
Lunar Pathfinder: the ESA 2021 article gives a 2024 launch target. Later secondary coverage suggests 2026, which was not confirmed. No navigation results were found.
The LCRNS page was last updated 17 February 2026 and carries a notice about a federal funding lapse, so its status may not be current.
